analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal jobs fund, paid for by a tax on stock and derivatives trades, to employ the jobless.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its 2013 introduction with 57 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in three House subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a Full Employment Trust Fund that pays for public jobs — repairing schools, parks and housing, staffing child care and Head Start, feeding programs — for people who are unemployed or stuck in part-time work. The money would come from a new tax on securities trading: 0.25 cents per dollar on stock trades and 0.02 cents on futures, swaps and credit default swaps, with retirement accounts and mutual funds exempt. If the fund ran short while unemployment was rising, the Federal Reserve would be required to lend it the difference.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and underemployed workers, especially the long-term unemployed, disadvantaged youth, and residents of high-poverty areas, would get paid jobs at prevailing wages with at least 12 months of employment. States, cities, tribes and community organizations would receive grants for public-works and human-services projects, and the existing workforce training system would get a dedicated funding stream.

how_it_helps.text: Grants would fund jobs in construction, housing repair, child care, Head Start staffing, parks, schools, emergency food programs and youth employment in communities with the highest unemployment and poverty.

Employers would have to pay workers at rates comparable to public-sector or prevailing local wages, at least 80 percent of grant money would go to wages, benefits and support services like child care, and the program could not be used to displace or lay off existing employees.

Jobs would last at least 12 months, 35 percent of workers hired would have to come from the long-term unemployed and other targeted groups, and workers would get help applying for benefits they qualify for.

The Fed would be required to lend the trust fund whatever is needed to keep national unemployment from rising more than one percentage point in a year, making the job program a standing commitment rather than a discretionary one.

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms and investors who trade stocks, futures, swaps, credit default swaps and options in the United States would pay the new transaction tax; the costs would fall most heavily on frequent traders and large institutions, since retirement accounts and mutual fund purchases are exempt.

drawbacks.text: The securities transaction tax would raise the cost of every taxable trade; critics argue that high-frequency and high-volume trading could shift to foreign exchanges to avoid the tax, reducing the revenue that funds the jobs program.

The bill requires the Federal Reserve to lend the trust fund whatever is needed to cap rising unemployment, which would inject direct political direction into monetary policy, a mandate that even supporters of aggressive job policy have disputed.

Public-service jobs can be slow to scale and the grants come with detailed labor rules, prevailing-wage requirements and arbitration procedures that add administrative cost and could limit how fast communities could put people to work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: During a period of elevated unemployment, a permanent, federally funded public jobs program at living wages would be a substantial benefit to workers and to communities getting real infrastructure and services built. The cost is a modest tax concentrated on securities trading, with an honest design concern: mandating Federal Reserve lending ties monetary policy to a statutory unemployment trigger, and the tax's durability depends on trading volume staying onshore. The bill is ambitious and lightly tested in drafting, but its central trade — a small tax on financial transactions funding direct employment — is clear and directional.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, sent to three subcommittees, and then sat there until the 113th Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on March 6, 2013, and it was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.

On April 23, 2013, it was referred to three subcommittees — Higher Education and Workforce Training, Workforce Protections, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — and the record shows no further action of any kind.
The bill had 57 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican support.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill never having received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities and derivatives traders are better off, since the transaction tax that would have funded the jobs program was never enacted. Unemployed workers gained nothing; the jobs program never started.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Securities traders; jobless workers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Training Act and recruited 57 cosponsors.

for.name: 57 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat beyond the cosponsor list moved it further and no Republican signed on.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill in March 2013 and sent it to subcommittees, where it received no hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, with jurisdiction over the bill's securities tax, never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 57 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a leading House Democrat; Republicans, who controlled both committees of referral, took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Securities and derivatives traders, including high-frequency trading firms
industries.note: The bill finances the jobs fund with a 0.25 percent tax on stock trades and 0.02 percent on futures, swaps and credit default swaps, with withholding on trades by foreign buyers. The cost falls on frequent, high-volume traders, and the industry has historically opposed such taxes; its gain in the bill's defeat was the tax never taking effect.

industries.industry: Job training and workforce development providers
industries.note: One third of the trust fund would flow through the existing Workforce Investment Act system, making workforce boards and training providers permanent channels for the new money. The bill also guarantees community-based organizations a quarter of the seats on state and local workforce boards.

industries.industry: State and local governments and Indian tribes
industries.note: They would receive grants to hire workers for public works, child care, parks and human services, with federal money covering most project costs.

Grant-funded jobs would pay prevailing or comparable public-sector wages and include construction work on schools, housing and public facilities, expanding paid work in these sectors without displacing existing employees.
